[PATH:theoretical] Systematic re-analysis of simulated ecosystem networks (e.g., using generalized Lotka-Volterra models) with controlled manipulation of trophic link strengths between disjoint cycles, measuring variance in species abundance and recovery rates after perturbation. — Directly tests the hypothesis by isolating the effect of weak vs. strong trophic links on resilience in multi-cycle topologies, allowing for causal inference and replication.

[PATH:empirical] Empirical data from well-characterized natural food webs (e.g., the Ythan Estuary or Chesapeake Bay) where disjoint cycles can be identified and link strengths estimated via stable isotope analysis or gut content analysis, combined with time-series resilience metrics. — Provides real-world validation of the theoretical prediction; if weak-link-connected cycles correlate with lower resilience indices (e.g., return time after disturbance), the hypothesis is supported; otherwise, refuted.

[PATH:literature] Literature review of prior theoretical studies on modularity, weak-link effects, and resilience in ecological networks (e.g., May's complexity-stability debate, Neutel et al. on weak trophic links). — Contextualizes the hypothesis within established theory; identifies whether existing models or empirical patterns already contradict or support the claim, and highlights gaps for new computational experiments.
